questions.question: What must exist before the phrase “inverse of $a$” makes sense in this setting?
options: An identity element.
A total order on the set.
A chosen basis of the set.
A determinant of the set.

questions.question: What does an inverse element do?
options: It makes $a$ leave the set.
It changes the operation into a commutative one.
It combines with $a$ to give $a$ again.
It combines with $a$ to give the identity element.

questions.question: Why does the definition include both $a\star a^{-1}=e$ and $a^{-1}\star a=e$?
options: Noncommutative operations need both inverses checked.
The two equations always have different identities.
The second equation checks associativity.
The inverse is not required to lie in the set.

questions.question: Under addition, what is the inverse of an element $a$?
Under multiplication, why is $0$ excluded when looking for multiplicative inverses in $\mathbb R$?
options: Because multiplication is not a binary operation on $\mathbb R$.
Because $0$ is not a real number.
There is no real number $b$ with $0\cdot b=1$.
Because $0$ has two different inverses.

questions.question: In $(\mathbb Z,+)$, what is the inverse of $7$?
In $(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},\cdot)$, what is the inverse of $2$?
For $a\star b=a+b+1$ on $\mathbb R$, the identity is $-1$. What is the inverse of $a$?
In $(\mathbb N,+)$ with positive natural numbers, why does $3$ have no inverse?
options: The additive inverse would be $-3$, which is not in $\mathbb N$.
Addition is not closed on $\mathbb N$.
The inverse would be $1/3$, which is always natural.
The inverse would be $3$, and $3$ is already in $\mathbb N$.

questions.question: Which element of $\{1,-1\}$ under multiplication is its own inverse?
options: Only $-1$.
Both $1$ and $-1$.
Neither element.
Only $1$.

questions.question: What is the difference between a left inverse and a right inverse?
options: A right inverse is the same as an identity element.
A left inverse gives $a$, while a right inverse gives $a^2$.
Left: $a^{-1}\star a=e$; right: $a\star a^{-1}=e$.
A left inverse exists only for commutative operations.

questions.question: If every element of a monoid has an inverse, what kind of structure is obtained?
options: A group.
A binary operation that is not closed.
A semigroup with no identity.
A vector space automatically.

questions.question: Why can the same element have different inverses under different operations?
options: An inverse is chosen by notation only.
The inverse never depends on the identity element.
The underlying set must change every time.
Both identity and inverse equation depend on the operation.

questions.question: What is the inverse of $-4$ in $(\mathbb R,+)$?
What is the inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ under matrix multiplication?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\0&1/3\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: In addition modulo $5$, what is the inverse of $3$?
Why is the notation $a^{-1}$ potentially misleading outside multiplication?
options: Inverse w.r.t. the chosen operation, not the reciprocal.
It always means the ordinary real reciprocal.
It always means the additive inverse.
It cannot be used in abstract algebra.

questions.question: Why must an inverse candidate belong to the same set $A$?
options: The definition requires $a^{-1}\in A$.
Because elements outside $A$ are automatically equal to the identity.
Because the operation is only associative outside $A$.
Because inverses are never outputs of the operation.

questions.question: In multiplication modulo $5$, what is the inverse of $2$?
For $a\star b=a+b-5$ on $\mathbb R$, the identity is $5$. What is the inverse of $a$?
